questions.explain: 5:45 am + 5:50 = 11:35 am. Adding the 20 minute drive: 11:55 am. Lunch is at 12:30 pm, which is 35 minutes after 11:55 am, so they arrive with 35 minutes to spare.

questions.prompt: A croc-safe swim session ends at 6:15 pm and dinner starts at 7:05 pm. The family spends 12 minutes driving home. How many minutes do they spend getting ready for dinner after the drive?
questions.explain: From 6:15 pm to 7:05 pm is 50 minutes in total. Subtracting the 12 minute drive leaves 50 - 12 = 38 minutes to get ready.

activity.title: Time Three Real Tasks and Total the Duration
activity.why: Proves they can accurately read start and end times off a real clock and calculate total duration across multiple tasks.
materials: a clock, watch or phone timer
steps: Pick three different everyday tasks to do back-to-back today (e.g. tidying your room, setting the table, walking the dog).
Before starting the first task, write down the exact start time (using am or pm) from a clock or phone.
Do each task and write down the exact time each one finishes and the next one starts.
Work out the duration in minutes for each of the three tasks.
Add all three durations together to find the total time spent.
Record your three individual durations and your total.

record.label: How many minutes did your first task take?
How many minutes did your second task take?
How many minutes did your third task take?
What was the total time for all three tasks, in minutes?
Explain which task took longest and whether your total added up correctly when you checked it.

activity.check: total_minutes should equal task1_minutes + task2_minutes + task3_minutes. Query it if the total doesn't add up.

lessons.title: Naming and Estimating Angles
lessons.curriculum_text: estimate and compare angles using angle names including acute, obtuse, straight angle, reflex and revolution, and recognise their relationship to a right angle
lessons.intro: Turning a boat's steering wheel, opening a gate, or watching the hands of a clock all involve angles, and giving them names helps us describe exactly how far something has turned.

sections.heading: What is an angle
sections.body:
An **angle** measures the amount of turn between two arms meeting at a point.

A small turn makes a small angle. A big turn, all the way around, makes a much bigger angle.

sections.heading: Naming angle types
sections.body:
Angles are named by comparing them to a **right angle**, which is a quarter turn (90°).

- An **acute** angle is smaller than a right angle.
- An **obtuse** angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle.
- A **straight angle** is a half turn (180°).
- A **reflex** angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than a full turn.
- A **revolution** is a full turn (360°).

sections.heading: Estimating angle size
sections.body:
You don't always need a protractor to describe an angle. Comparing it to a right angle is often enough: is it clearly smaller, clearly bigger, or close to a right angle?

Think about a door opening. A little bit open is acute. Opened flat against the wall is close to a straight angle.

key_points: An angle measures the amount of turn between two arms meeting at a point.
A right angle is a quarter turn (90 degrees).
Acute angles are smaller than a right angle. Obtuse angles are bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle.
A straight angle is a half turn (180 degrees). A reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than a full turn (360 degrees).
lessons.try_this: Join two straws, paddle-pop sticks or pencils at one end with your fingers holding them together. Make different sized angles and sort them into acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex.

questions.prompt: What is a right angle?
questions.explain: A right angle measures 90 degrees, which is a quarter of a full 360 degree turn.

questions.prompt: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle.
questions.explain: Acute angles are always smaller than 90 degrees, the size of a right angle.

questions.prompt: A door is pushed open wider than a right angle, but not yet open flat against the wall. What type of angle does it form?
questions.explain: Obtuse angles sit between 90 degrees (a right angle) and 180 degrees (a straight angle), which matches a door opened past a right angle but not flat.

questions.prompt: A door is pushed all the way open until it lies flat against the wall. Does the angle it forms measure 180 degrees?
questions.explain: A straight angle is a half turn, which is 180 degrees — exactly what a door flat against the wall forms.

questions.prompt: The corner of a square picture frame forms a right angle. How many degrees is that?
questions.explain: A right angle is a quarter turn, which equals 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: A tinnie spins around so far that it turns more than a straight line, but doesn't quite make it all the way back around to a full circle. What type of angle best describes this turn?
questions.explain: A reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle (180 degrees) but smaller than a full revolution (360 degrees), matching a turn beyond a straight line but short of a full circle.

questions.prompt: A ceiling fan blade spins all the way around once, back to exactly where it started. How many degrees has it turned through?
questions.explain: A revolution is a complete turn all the way around, which equals 360 degrees.

questions.prompt: At exactly 3 o'clock, what type of angle do the hour hand and minute hand of a clock form?
questions.explain: At 3 o'clock, the hour hand points to the 3 and the minute hand points to the 12, forming exactly a 90 degree right angle.

questions.prompt: At 10 o'clock, what is the size, in degrees, of the smaller angle between the clock's hour and minute hands?
questions.explain: At 10 o'clock, the hour hand points to the 10 (which is 300 degrees around from 12) and the minute hand points to 12 (0 degrees). The smaller angle between them is 360 - 300 = 60 degrees.

questions.prompt: A revolving lighthouse beam completes 3 full revolutions in one minute. How many degrees does it turn through in total during that minute?
questions.explain: One revolution is 360 degrees. Three revolutions is 3 x 360 = 1080 degrees.

questions.prompt: A door starts closed (0°) and is opened until it forms a reflex angle. Which of these opening amounts could it be?
questions.explain: A reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle (180°) but smaller than a full revolution (360°). 45° is acute, 90° is right, and 170° is obtuse - only 210° is reflex.

questions.prompt: Two angles sit next to each other along a straight line, together making a straight angle of 180°. If one of the angles is 65°, how many degrees is the other?
questions.explain: Since the two angles together make a straight angle of 180°, the other angle is 180 - 65 = 115°.

activity.title: Angle Hunt: Measure Real Angles Around You
activity.why: Proves they can estimate and then verify real angles found in the world, not just angles drawn on paper.
materials: a protractor (paper, plastic, or a protractor app)
steps: Walk around your house or yard and find 4 different real angles - for example, a gate opened partway, a door ajar, a branch meeting a trunk, or a fence corner.
Before measuring, look at each one and guess whether it's acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex.
Use your protractor to measure the actual angle in degrees for each of the 4 angles.
Write down your estimate and the actual measured degrees for each of the 4 angles.
Check how close your estimates were to the real measurements.
Record the actual degree measurements for your first two angles below.

record.label: What was the actual measurement of your first angle, in degrees?
What was the actual measurement of your second angle, in degrees?
What type was your first angle?
Describe the 4 real angles you found and how close your estimates were to the actual measurements.

activity.check: angle1_type should match the degree range for angle1_degrees (e.g. under 90 = acute). Query a mismatch.
